Q001040:
## Amazon Inspector
Amazon Inspector is a managed vulnerability scanner.
- **EC2**: it uses the **SSM Agent** already on instances to inventory software packages and match them against CVEs; no extra scanner agent is needed. An agentless option also exists for instances without the agent.
- **ECR**: it scans container images on push and continuously afterwards.
- **Continuous rescans**: when a new CVE is published, affected resources are rescanned automatically.
- **Risk score**: each finding gets an Inspector score that adjusts the CVSS base score, for example raising it when the instance is reachable from the internet.
## Organization-wide
In AWS Organizations you pick a **delegated administrator** account, which can enable Inspector for all member accounts, auto-enable new accounts and see every finding in one place.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Inspector org-wide (correct):** it continuously scans EC2 through the existing SSM Agent and ECR images, rescans on new CVEs, prioritizes by reachability, and a delegated administrator runs it across all 40 accounts.
- ✗ **B. Config rules for package versions:** Config records configuration, not vulnerability data, so you would have to build and update your own CVE matching logic, and there is no built-in ECR image scanning or exposure scoring.
- ✗ **C. Weekly third-party scanner AMI:** scans only once a week, misses CVEs published in between, and adds scanner instances in 40 accounts to launch, license and maintain.
- ✗ **D. GuardDuty Malware Protection:** it looks for malicious files on EBS volumes and other storage when triggered, not for known software vulnerabilities (CVEs) in packages or images.

## Key idea
Continuous CVE scanning for EC2 and container images across an organization is Amazon Inspector, not a threat detector like GuardDuty or a config tracker like Config.
Q001043:
## AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS)
DRS protects physical servers, VMware VMs and cloud instances by replicating them to AWS.
- An **agent** on each source server sends **continuous block-level replication** to a low-cost staging area in your AWS account, giving an RPO of seconds.
- On failover, DRS launches **recovery instances** from the latest or an earlier point in time, typically within minutes, with no application changes.
- You can run **drills** at any time without stopping replication, and fail back to the source environment afterwards.
Example: a VMware SQL Server VM is replicated continuously; during an outage it is launched as an EC2 instance from the state a few seconds before the failure.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. AWS Backup:** it takes scheduled backups, so the RPO is the backup interval, and it does not replicate on-premises VMware servers continuously for minute-level failover.
- ✗ **B. Application Migration Service for one-time migration:** MGN is built for cutting servers over once; it is not the service for ongoing DR with repeated drills, point-in-time recovery and failback.
- ✗ **C. DataSync:** it copies files and objects between storage systems; it does not replicate server disks or launch recovery instances.
- ✓ **D. Elastic Disaster Recovery (correct):** it continuously replicates whole servers at block level and launches them on EC2 within minutes, which is exactly lift-and-shift DR without re-architecting.

## Key idea
For continuous server replication to AWS with minutes of recovery time, use Elastic Disaster Recovery; backups, migration and file copy tools serve other goals.
Q001050:
## How Route 53 failover routing works
Route 53 failover routing uses two records with the same name: one marked **primary** and one marked **secondary**. A Route 53 health check is attached to the primary (for example an HTTPS check on `/health` of the us-east-1 load balancer).
- While the health check passes, Route 53 answers DNS queries with the primary.
- When it fails for the configured number of checks, Route 53 automatically answers with the secondary (the us-west-2 endpoint).
- When the primary recovers, answers switch back.
## Things to tune
- Keep the record TTL short (for example 60 seconds) so resolvers pick up the change quickly. Alias records to AWS load balancers use the target's TTL.
- Health checkers run from several locations, so a single checker failing does not trigger failover.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Simple routing plus runbook:** simple routing has no health-check-driven switching, so failover waits for a person to follow the runbook and change the record.
- ✓ **B. Failover routing with health checks (correct):** Route 53 itself detects the unhealthy primary and returns the standby record, so no one has to edit DNS during an incident.
- ✗ **C. Weighted 50/50:** it sends half of all traffic to the standby at all times, which is not an active-passive design, and without health checks on each record it would keep sending users to a failed Region.
- ✗ **D. Manual CNAME change:** it depends on an on-call engineer noticing and editing DNS, which adds delay and human error and is exactly what the requirement rules out.

## Key idea
Automatic DNS failover means failover records plus a health check on the primary; simple, weighted-without-checks or manual changes do not switch by themselves.
Q001051:
## Aurora Global Database
An Aurora Global Database has one primary cluster in one Region and read-only secondary clusters in other Regions. Replication happens at the **storage layer**, not through MySQL binlogs, using dedicated infrastructure, with little impact on database performance.
- Typical replication lag is under one second, which gives an RPO of seconds.
- During a regional outage you can fail over (or detach and promote) a secondary to a full read/write cluster, typically within minutes.
- A planned **switchover** swaps primary and secondary roles without data loss, useful for DR drills.
Example: primary in `eu-west-1`, secondary in `eu-central-1` serving local reads; if `eu-west-1` fails, promote `eu-central-1` and point the application at its writer endpoint.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Binlog replicas plus snapshots:** binlog replication runs through the database engine and lags more under heavy writes, and 15-minute snapshot exports imply an RPO measured in minutes rather than seconds.
- ✓ **B. Aurora Global Database (correct):** storage-level cross-Region replication gives sub-second lag and a promotable secondary, matching an RPO of seconds and fast Region recovery.
- ✗ **C. Daily manual backup copies:** the RPO is up to a day, and restoring a cluster from a snapshot takes far longer than promoting a replica.
- ✗ **D. Serverless v2 with auto-pause:** auto-pause only scales idle capacity to zero; two independent clusters have no replication between them, so it provides no DR at all.

## Key idea
For seconds of RPO and fast promotion across Regions, use Aurora Global Database, not binlog replicas, snapshots or unconnected clusters.
Q001077:
## Deploying the same stack to many accounts
AWS CloudFormation **StackSets** deploy one template as stack instances into many accounts and Regions from a single place (the management account or a delegated administrator).
StackSets has two permission models:
- **Self-managed**: you create the administration and execution IAM roles in each target account yourself.
- **Service-managed**: StackSets uses trusted access with AWS Organizations and creates the needed roles for you. You target **organizational units (OUs)** instead of listing account IDs.
## Automatic deployment
With service-managed permissions you can turn on **automatic deployment**: when an account is added to a targeted OU, StackSets deploys the stack there, and when it leaves the OU the stack can be removed or retained.
Updating the template in the stack set rolls the change out to every stack instance, with controls such as maximum concurrent accounts and failure tolerance.
Example: a stack set with a baseline VPC, a CloudTrail trail and guardrail IAM roles targets the `Workloads` OU; a new account moved into that OU gets the baseline within minutes.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Config rules with auto-remediation:** Config detects and fixes non-compliant configuration, but it is not a way to provision and version a baseline of VPCs, logging and IAM resources in every account.
- ✗ **B. Manual stack per account:** deploying by hand in 40 accounts is slow and error-prone, does not reach new accounts automatically, and makes central updates a 40-step job.
- ✗ **C. Custom Lambda on account creation:** it could work, but it rebuilds what StackSets already provides (cross-account roles, controlled rollout, central updates, drift detection) as custom code that the team must maintain, and it does not handle accounts moving between OUs.
- ✓ **D. StackSets with service-managed permissions (correct):** targeting OUs with automatic deployment covers both current and future accounts, and one update to the stack set rolls out centrally to all of them without per-account role setup.

## Key idea
For the same resources in every current and future account of an OU, use StackSets with service-managed permissions and automatic deployment rather than per-account or custom provisioning.
Q001078:
## Cross-account CloudFormation deployments
A common pattern keeps CI/CD in a **tooling account** and deploys to separate workload accounts. Two IAM roles in the production account do the work:
- A **cross-account role** that the pipeline assumes. Its trust policy allows the tooling account's pipeline role, and its permissions are narrow: pass a specific role to CloudFormation, create or update specific stacks, and read the artifact bucket (plus `kms:Decrypt` on the artifact key).
- A **CloudFormation service role** that CloudFormation itself uses to create the stack's resources. Only CloudFormation can assume it, and it holds the permissions the template needs.
## Why two roles
The pipeline never gets the power to create resources directly; it can only ask CloudFormation to deploy with the approved service role (`iam:PassRole` limited to that role ARN).
Example: `arn:aws:iam::222233334444:role/PipelineDeployRole` may call `cloudformation:UpdateStack` on `app-prod` and pass `CfnExecRole`, which holds the EC2, ECS and RDS permissions.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. AdministratorAccess:** this is the broad permission the requirement forbids. A compromised pipeline or a bad commit could change anything in production.
- ✓ **B. Scoped cross-account role plus service role (correct):** the pipeline assumes a narrowly scoped role in production that can only drive CloudFormation, and the resource permissions live in a CloudFormation service role, so the pipeline itself never holds broad IAM rights in production.
- ✗ **C. Root credentials in Secrets Manager:** root credentials cannot be scoped at all, and AWS recommends not using the root user for everyday tasks or automation. Storing them for a pipeline is the widest possible access.
- ✗ **D. Move the pipeline into production:** it does not reduce the permissions the pipeline needs, and it mixes build tooling into the production account, undoing the account separation.

## Key idea
Cross-account deployments should use a narrow assumable role that only drives CloudFormation, with resource permissions held by a CloudFormation service role, not admin rights for the pipeline.
Q001081:
## Why builds repeat work
Each CodeBuild build runs in a fresh container, so by default every build downloads all dependencies again, such as `node_modules`, Maven `.m2` artifacts, pip wheels or Docker base layers.
## CodeBuild caching
- **Amazon S3 cache**: paths listed under `cache: paths:` in the `buildspec.yml` are uploaded to an S3 bucket at the end of a build and restored at the start of the next one. It works across build hosts.
- **Local cache**: stored on the build host and reused only while the same host is available. Modes are **source cache** (Git metadata), **Docker layer cache** and **custom cache** (directories you choose).
Example buildspec fragment: `cache: paths: - '/root/.m2/**/*'`. A build that spent 25 minutes resolving Maven dependencies may finish in a few minutes when the cache is warm, because only changed dependencies are fetched.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Persistent EC2 build server:** it could keep dependencies around, but it gives up CodeBuild's managed, clean and scalable build environments and adds a server to patch and scale, while CodeBuild caching gets the same benefit.
- ✓ **B. CodeBuild caching (correct):** persisting dependency directories in an S3 or local cache means each build restores them instead of downloading everything again, which directly removes the step that makes the build slow.
- ✗ **C. More parallel stages:** parallel stages help when there are independent jobs. Each stage would still reinstall all dependencies, so the slow step remains and may run several times.
- ✗ **D. Largest compute type:** dependency download time is dominated by network and repository fetches, not CPU. A bigger instance costs more per minute and barely shortens the reinstall.

## Key idea
When builds are slow because they fetch the same dependencies each time, cache them in CodeBuild instead of adding compute or parallelism.
Q001083:
## How UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED happens
When a stack update fails, CloudFormation rolls the resources back to their previous state. If the rollback itself cannot complete, the stack stops in `UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED`. Typical causes: a resource was changed or deleted outside CloudFormation, a dependency (such as a security group) is still in use, or permissions or limits changed.
In this state you cannot update the stack until the rollback is finished.
## Continuing the rollback
The **ContinueUpdateRollback** action (console: "Continue update rollback", CLI: `aws cloudformation continue-update-rollback`) retries the rollback. First fix the underlying cause if you can. For resources that still cannot roll back, pass them in `--resources-to-skip`; CloudFormation marks them as rolled back so the stack can reach `UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE`.
Example: `aws cloudformation continue-update-rollback --stack-name app --resources-to-skip MyDBParameterGroup`. Afterwards you make the skipped resource consistent with the template, often through a follow-up update.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Edit resources, then retry the update:** the stack cannot be updated while it is in `UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED`. The rollback has to be completed first; fixing resources by hand only helps as a step before continuing the rollback.
- ✗ **B. Wait for an automatic retry:** CloudFormation does not retry a failed rollback on its own. The stack stays in this state until someone continues the rollback or deletes the stack.
- ✓ **C. ContinueUpdateRollback with skipped resources (correct):** it is the supported way to finish a failed rollback, optionally skipping the resources that cannot roll back, and it returns the stack to a state where normal updates work again.
- ✗ **D. Delete and recreate everything:** deletion is a heavy, risky last resort that can destroy data and cause downtime. It is unnecessary when the rollback can be continued.

## Key idea
A stack in `UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED` is recovered with ContinueUpdateRollback (skipping stuck resources if needed), not by retrying the update, waiting, or deleting the stack.
Q001084:
## Blue/green deployments for ECS with CodeDeploy
With the CodeDeploy deployment controller, an ECS service has two **task sets** behind an Application Load Balancer: the current (blue) set and the new (green) set. CodeDeploy starts the green tasks, then moves listener traffic from blue to green using a deployment configuration:
- **All-at-once**: everything moves in one step.
- **Canary**: for example `ECSCanary10Percent5Minutes`, 10% first, the rest after 5 minutes.
- **Linear**: for example `ECSLinear10PercentEvery1Minutes`, 10% more every minute.
## Automatic rollback
The deployment group can list **CloudWatch alarms** (such as 5xx rate or latency). If an alarm goes into ALARM during the deployment, CodeDeploy stops it and shifts traffic back to the blue task set. Lifecycle hooks can also run validation Lambda functions between steps.
## ECS's own deployment options
The native ECS deployment controller now also offers blue/green, canary and linear strategies. A **rolling update** replaces tasks in batches and can roll back through the deployment circuit breaker or CloudWatch alarms, but it does not shift traffic by percentage to a separate new task set.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. New cluster and manual DNS switch:** it is manual, DNS changes take effect unevenly because of caching, and there is no alarm-driven automatic rollback.
- ✓ **B. CodeDeploy blue/green for ECS (correct):** it provides gradual (linear or canary) traffic shifting between task sets and automatic rollback on CloudWatch alarms as configuration, so no custom scripting is needed.
- ✗ **C. Adjust desired count and watch logs:** this is a manual process with no controlled traffic percentages and no automatic rollback, the opposite of minimal scripting.
- ✗ **D. Plain rolling update:** a rolling update replaces tasks in batches within one service and can roll back on alarms, but traffic is not shifted by percentage between a separate old and new task set, so it does not provide the gradual, controlled shift this design asks for.

## Key idea
For gradual traffic shifting between ECS task sets with alarm-based rollback and little scripting, use CodeDeploy blue/green with a linear or canary configuration.
Q001085:
## Self-service without broad permissions
**AWS Service Catalog** lets a central team publish approved products for others to launch:
- A **product** is a CloudFormation template (or Terraform configuration) with versions, such as "three-tier web app".
- A **portfolio** groups products and is shared with IAM users, groups or roles, or with other accounts in the organization.
- A **launch constraint** names an IAM role that Service Catalog uses to create the resources. End users need only permission to use Service Catalog, not to create EC2, RDS or IAM resources themselves.
- **Template constraints** limit parameters, for example allowing only `t3.small` or `t3.medium`.
## Example
A developer opens the portfolio, picks "Web app v3", enters an app name and environment, and Service Catalog provisions the stack with the launch role. The developer can update or terminate it, but cannot create an arbitrary resource outside the product.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Publicly shared Automation documents:** sharing documents publicly exposes internal runbooks to everyone and does not give a governed, versioned product catalog; users running them still need the permissions the documents use.
- ✗ **B. CreateStack-only permissions:** CloudFormation creates resources with the caller's permissions unless a service role is used, so developers could submit any template, and to succeed they would still need rights to the underlying resources.
- ✓ **C. Service Catalog with CloudFormation products (correct):** developers self-serve from a curated list of approved architectures, and launch constraints let the resources be created by a separate role, so developers never hold direct permissions to create arbitrary resources.
- ✗ **D. Read-only access plus tickets:** it avoids broad permissions but removes self-service; every environment waits on a manual ticket.

## Key idea
Service Catalog gives self-service provisioning of approved templates while a launch role, not the developer, holds the resource permissions.
Q001093:
## S3 replication
S3 replication copies objects automatically and asynchronously from a source bucket to one or more destination buckets. It requires versioning on both buckets and an IAM role that S3 uses to copy objects.
- **Cross-Region Replication (CRR)**: destination bucket in a different Region, used for compliance, lower-latency access or disaster recovery.
- **Same-Region Replication (SRR)**: destination in the same Region, used for log aggregation or copies between accounts.
- Rules can filter by prefix or tag, change the storage class or owner of replicas, and **S3 Replication Time Control** adds a replication SLA (99.99% of objects within 15 minutes) with metrics.
- Replication applies to new objects after the rule is created; **S3 Batch Replication** copies existing objects.
Example: a rule copies `patient-records/` from `us-east-1` to a bucket in `us-west-2` in the `S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval` storage class.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. S3 Cross-Region Replication (correct):** it copies new objects automatically and asynchronously to a bucket in another Region, meeting the requirement for a separate-Region copy without scripts.
- ✗ **B. Same-Region Replication only:** the copies stay in the same Region, so a Regional event affects both, which fails the separate-Region requirement.
- ✗ **C. Nightly CLI sync:** it is manual or scripted rather than built-in replication, leaves up to a day of new objects uncopied, and depends on the job running successfully.
- ✗ **D. Transfer Acceleration:** it speeds up uploads and downloads over long distances through edge locations; it does not copy objects to another bucket or Region.

## Key idea
For automatic copies of new S3 objects in another Region, use Cross-Region Replication; SRR stays in-Region and Transfer Acceleration only speeds up transfers.
Q001101:
## Two sides of cross-account access
When a principal in one account accesses a resource in another account, **both accounts must allow it**:
- The **identity policy** in Account B lets its role call `s3:GetObject` on the bucket.
- A **resource-based policy** in Account A (the bucket policy) lets that external principal in.
If either side is missing, the request is denied. Within a single account, one allow is enough; across accounts, the resource owner must agree too.
## A least-privilege bucket policy
Example statement on the bucket in Account A:
- Principal: `arn:aws:iam::222222222222:role/analytics-reader`
- Actions: `s3:GetObject` (and `s3:ListBucket` on the bucket if listing is needed)
- Resource: `arn:aws:s3:::producer-data/*`
Naming the specific role instead of the whole account keeps access tight. If the objects use SSE-KMS, the KMS key policy must also allow that role to decrypt.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. IAM policy in Account B only:** an identity policy in Account B cannot grant access to a resource Account A owns. Without an allow in the bucket policy, S3 denies the request.
- ✓ **B. Bucket policy granting the Account B role read access (correct):** the bucket owner explicitly allows only the named role to read, which, combined with the role's own identity policy, completes cross-account access with least privilege.
- ✗ **C. Daily copy job:** copying data creates stale duplicates, extra storage cost and another pipeline to run, and the copy job itself would still need cross-account permissions.
- ✗ **D. Root user full access:** granting Account B's root user full access to Account A is the opposite of least privilege, and an IAM policy in Account A cannot grant permissions to another account's principals anyway.
- ✗ **E. Public bucket:** a public bucket lets anyone on the internet read the data. An obscure bucket name is not access control, and S3 Block Public Access is designed to prevent exactly this.

## Key idea
Cross-account access needs an allow on both sides: the consumer's identity policy and the owner's resource policy naming the specific role.
Q001102:
## How Secrets Manager rotation works
AWS Secrets Manager stores a secret (for example the username and password of an RDS database) and can rotate it on a schedule, such as every 30 days.
- For RDS, Aurora and other supported databases, an AWS-provided rotation Lambda function (created from a rotation template) creates a new password, sets it on the database, tests it, and marks it as the current version (`AWSCURRENT`).
- Applications do not store the password. They call `GetSecretValue` at runtime (often with a client-side cache), so they automatically pick up the new value.
- The **alternating users** strategy keeps two database users and switches between them, so one valid login always exists during rotation.
For the RDS master password, RDS can also manage the secret in Secrets Manager directly with `ManageMasterUserPassword` (managed rotation, no Lambda function to maintain).

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Encrypted config file and monthly redeploy:** the rotation depends on a person changing values and redeploying, which is manual work, risks mistakes, and a redeploy may cause disruption.
- ✗ **B. Manual console rotation:** someone must change the password and update the application at the same moment. Any gap between the two causes failed logins, and the process can be forgotten.
- ✓ **C. Secrets Manager with automatic RDS rotation (correct):** rotation runs on the 30-day schedule without people, updates the database password and the secret together, and applications read the current value at runtime, so no redeploy or config change is needed.
- ✗ **D. Parameter Store SecureString with expiration:** Parameter Store has no built-in rotation. An expiration policy (advanced parameters only) can delete the parameter or send a notification, but it does not generate a new password or change it on the database.

## Key idea
Secrets Manager rotates the database password and the stored secret together, and apps that fetch the secret at runtime never need a manual update.
Q001104:
## Scaling policy types in EC2 Auto Scaling
- **Target tracking**: you pick a metric and a target, such as average CPU utilization at 50 percent. Auto Scaling creates and manages the CloudWatch alarms itself and adds or removes instances in proportion to how far the metric is from the target.
- **Step scaling**: you define alarms and a table of adjustments, for example add 2 instances at 70 percent and 4 at 85 percent.
- **Simple scaling**: one alarm, one fixed adjustment, then a cooldown before the next action.
- **Scheduled scaling**: changes capacity at set times, useful for predictable daily patterns.
## Example
With a target of 50 percent and 4 instances at 75 percent CPU, target tracking calculates roughly how many instances bring the average back to 50 percent and adds them, then scales in more cautiously once load falls.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Step scaling with multiple alarms:** it can react to varying load, but the team must define every alarm threshold and step adjustment and keep tuning them, which is exactly what they want to avoid.
- ✓ **B. Target tracking on average CPU (correct):** it keeps CPU near the chosen value automatically and needs no thresholds or step tables, which fits unpredictable load and the team's wish not to define them.
- ✗ **C. Scheduled scaling:** scheduled actions change capacity at fixed times. The load here is unpredictable, so the schedule would not match when CPU actually rises.
- ✗ **D. Simple scaling with one alarm:** the team still sets the threshold and adjustment size, and the fixed step plus cooldown reacts coarsely and slowly to fluctuating load.

## Key idea
To hold a metric near a value without writing thresholds, use target tracking; step and simple scaling require you to design the alarms and adjustments yourself.
Q001111:
## Lifecycle hooks
An Auto Scaling **lifecycle hook** pauses an instance during launch or termination so you can run custom actions.
- A termination hook moves the instance to `Terminating:Wait` instead of terminating it right away.
- The hook sends a notification through Amazon EventBridge, SNS or SQS, or the instance can detect it itself, and a script deregisters from the service registry and finishes in-flight requests.
- The script calls `complete-lifecycle-action` with result `CONTINUE`; the instance then terminates. If nothing responds, the heartbeat timeout (default 3,600 seconds) ends the wait and the default result applies.
Example: the instance removes itself from a Consul or Cloud Map registry, waits 30 seconds for requests to finish, then completes the hook.
## Related settings
Load balancer **deregistration delay** drains connections from a target group, but only a lifecycle hook gives time for custom steps such as registry deregistration.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Termination lifecycle hook (correct):** it holds the instance in a wait state during scale-in so the application can deregister and flush requests, then the instance terminates once the action is completed or the timeout ends.
- ✗ **B. Longer health check grace period:** the grace period delays health checks after an instance launches. It has no effect on how an instance is terminated during scale-in.
- ✗ **C. Termination protection:** EC2 termination protection does not stop Auto Scaling from terminating instances, and the Auto Scaling equivalent, scale-in protection, blocks scale-in instead of giving a graceful shutdown window.
- ✗ **D. Longer cooldown:** cooldowns space out scaling activities. They do not delay the termination of an individual instance, so the app still gets no time to drain.

## Key idea
To run shutdown steps before an Auto Scaling instance terminates, use a termination lifecycle hook; grace periods, cooldowns and protection settings do not provide a drain window.
Q001118:
## Why metrics hide slow calls
CloudWatch metrics are aggregates, such as average latency per service per minute. If 2 percent of requests are slow because one downstream call occasionally takes 3 seconds, averages barely move.
## Distributed tracing with X-Ray
AWS X-Ray follows single requests across services:
- Each request gets a **trace ID**, passed along in the `X-Amzn-Trace-Id` header.
- Each service records a **segment** with its timing, and **subsegments** for downstream calls such as a DynamoDB query or an HTTP call to another service.
- The **trace map** shows services and their latencies and errors; a single trace's timeline shows exactly which hop took the time.
Services are instrumented with OpenTelemetry (AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry, which AWS now recommends over the older X-Ray SDKs), and Lambda, API Gateway and others can enable tracing with a setting. CloudWatch Application Signals builds on the same trace data.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. More CPU alarms:** CPU utilization says whether a host is busy, not which call in a request chain is slow. A slow downstream dependency often causes no CPU increase at all.
- ✗ **B. VPC Flow Logs with manual correlation:** flow logs record IP connections and bytes, not application requests or their latency, and correlating timestamps by hand across services is slow and imprecise.
- ✓ **C. X-Ray tracing across the services (correct):** traces show each request's path and the time spent in every segment, so the specific slow service call can be identified even when aggregate metrics look normal.
- ✗ **D. 1-second high-resolution metrics:** finer metrics are still aggregates per service. They show when latency rises but not which call inside a specific request was slow.

## Key idea
To find the slow hop in a distributed request, trace individual requests (X-Ray); metrics and alarms only show aggregates.
Q001123:
## Why a cache in front of DynamoDB
DynamoDB serves reads in single-digit milliseconds at almost any scale. Some workloads need more: a few extremely hot keys read millions of times per minute, where every read still goes to the storage partitions and each partition has its own throughput limits.
## How DAX works
**DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX)** is a managed, in-memory, write-through cache cluster that sits in your VPC in front of a table.
- It speaks the DynamoDB API, so the app swaps the DynamoDB client for the DAX client and keeps calls like `GetItem`, `Query` and `BatchGetItem`.
- Cached eventually consistent reads return in **microseconds**; misses are read from the table and stored in the item cache or query cache.
- Writes go through DAX to the table, keeping the cache current.
Example: a leaderboard key read 50,000 times per second is served from DAX memory instead of hitting one hot partition.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. On-demand capacity alone:** on-demand changes how you pay for and scale throughput, but every read still hits the table at millisecond latency, and hot keys still concentrate on a partition.
- ✗ **B. Memcached with custom invalidation as the only option:** ElastiCache can cache DynamoDB data, but you must write and maintain cache-aside and invalidation code, and it is clearly not the only viable option because DAX does this natively.
- ✓ **C. DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) (correct):** it is the purpose-built, API-compatible cache for DynamoDB, turning millisecond reads of hot keys into microsecond reads with minimal code change and no custom invalidation logic.
- ✗ **D. Global Tables:** Global Tables replicate a table across Regions for multi-Region writes and resilience; reads in each Region still take milliseconds and hot keys remain hot.

## Key idea
For microsecond reads of hot DynamoDB keys with minimal code change, use DAX; capacity modes and Global Tables change scaling and geography, not read latency.
Q001142:
## Central backups with AWS Backup
**AWS Backup** creates and manages backups for many services (EC2, EBS, RDS, Aurora, DynamoDB, EFS and more) through **backup plans** that set schedule, retention and copy rules.
- With AWS Organizations, **backup policies** attached to OUs push the same plans into every member account, with resources selected by tags.
- **Cross-account copy** sends recovery points to a vault in a dedicated backup account in the same organization.
- **AWS Backup Vault Lock** in compliance mode makes that vault WORM: recovery points cannot be deleted or have retention shortened, even by the account's administrators.
Example: a policy on the `Prod` OU backs up every resource tagged `backup=daily` and copies each recovery point to a locked vault in a separate backup account.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** Org-wide Backup policies with cross-account copies to a Vault Lock vault: one policy governs all accounts and services, and a locked vault in an isolated account survives ransomware or a compromised source account.
- ✗ **B. DataSync nightly exports:** DataSync moves files and objects, not consistent point-in-time backups of RDS, DynamoDB or EC2 volumes, and it provides no retention policy or restore workflow.
- ✗ **C. Native snapshots per service and account:** each team configures its own schedule and retention, so coverage is inconsistent and copies stay in the same accounts an attacker could compromise.
- ✗ **D. Default 7-day RDS retention:** it covers only RDS, keeps backups in the same account, and a short retention does not protect against a compromise noticed later.

## Key idea
For multi-account, multi-service backup governance, use AWS Backup policies with cross-account copies into a locked vault in an isolated account.
Q001143:
## Preventive versus detective controls
- **Detective** controls, such as AWS Config rules, report a violation after the resource exists.
- **Preventive** controls stop the API call before anything is created.
## Service control policies
An **SCP** attached to an OU sets the maximum permissions for every IAM user and role in its accounts, including account root users. A deny in an SCP cannot be overridden by any IAM policy in those accounts.
Using the global condition key `aws:RequestedRegion`, an SCP can deny actions outside approved Regions:
`"Condition": {"StringNotEquals": {"aws:RequestedRegion": ["eu-west-1","eu-central-1"]}}`
For S3 bucket creation, teams often also check `s3:LocationConstraint`. SCPs do not apply to the management account, so workloads are kept in member accounts.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Config rule:** it only flags resources that already exist in the wrong Region, so data may already be stored there before anyone reacts.
- ✗ **B. Permissions boundaries per user:** they must be applied to every user and role individually and can be missed or removed by account administrators, so they are not an organization-wide guarantee.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** OU-level SCP on aws:RequestedRegion: requests to create S3 buckets or RDS instances in other Regions are denied before anything is created, for every principal in every account under the OU.
- ✗ **D. EventBridge auto-delete:** this reacts after creation, so data can land in the wrong Region, and automated deletion can fail or destroy data.

## Key idea
To prevent, not detect, Region use across an organization, deny it with an SCP on `aws:RequestedRegion`.
Q001188:
## Workforce sign-in across many accounts
**AWS IAM Identity Center** is the recommended way to give employees single sign-on access to many AWS accounts in AWS Organizations.
- **Identity source**: Identity Center can use Active Directory, either through **AWS Managed Microsoft AD** with a trust to on-premises AD or through **AD Connector**, or an external SAML identity provider.
- **Permission sets** define what a user or group can do; they are assigned to groups per account, and Identity Center creates the matching IAM roles in each account.
- Users sign in once at the access portal and choose an account and role, getting short-term credentials.
## Example
An AD group `Finance-Admins` gets the `FinanceAdmin` permission set on three accounts. When someone joins that AD group, access follows automatically, with no per-account IAM users.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Separate SAML trust per account:** this can work, but each account needs its own identity provider trust and roles, which is hard to manage and audit at 2,000 users and many accounts.
- ✓ **B. IAM Identity Center with the existing AD (correct):** employees use their AD credentials once and reach many accounts through centrally managed permission sets, with no IAM users per account.
- ✗ **C. Cognito user pools per account:** Cognito provides sign-in for customers of your applications; it is not the tool for workforce access to AWS accounts and would add separate directories to maintain.
- ✗ **D. IAM users with the same password everywhere:** this creates thousands of long-term credentials to manage, bypasses AD, and violates the goal of avoiding IAM users.

## Key idea
Workforce SSO to many accounts from existing AD is IAM Identity Center; Cognito serves application users and per-account IAM users defeat the purpose.
Q001196:
## ECS capacity options
An ECS task needs compute to run on. The main options are:
- **EC2 launch type** (or EC2 capacity providers): tasks run on EC2 instances in your account. You choose instance types and AMIs, patch them and scale the cluster, and you pay for the instances whether or not they are full.
- **AWS Fargate**: serverless compute for containers. You specify CPU and memory per task; AWS provisions, patches and scales the underlying capacity. Billing is for the vCPU and memory each task requests while it runs.
- **ECS Anywhere**: tasks run on your own servers outside AWS, managed from ECS.
## Trade-off
Fargate removes instance management in exchange for less control: no access to the host, no custom AMIs, and fewer hardware choices, such as no GPUs.
Example: a nightly batch job requests 2 vCPU and 4 GB for 20 minutes; with Fargate the team pays for those 20 minutes and never sees a server.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. AWS Fargate launch type (correct):** it runs each task without any EC2 instances for the team to manage, patch or scale, and bills per task based on requested resources.
- ✗ **B. EC2 launch type with Spot only:** Spot lowers cost, but the team still manages, patches and scales the instances, plus handles interruptions.
- ✗ **C. EC2 launch type with manual Auto Scaling:** this adds instance management and manual scaling, the exact work the team wants to avoid.
- ✗ **D. ECS Anywhere:** tasks run on the company's own infrastructure, so it keeps all server management on premises.

## Key idea
For containers with no servers to manage and per-task billing, use Fargate; any EC2-backed option keeps instance operations with you.
Q001215:
## How CodePipeline moves artifacts
Every action in a pipeline reads and writes **artifacts**: zip files kept in an S3 bucket called the **artifact store**. The store is encrypted with a KMS key, either the AWS managed `aws/s3` key or a customer managed key.
## Cross-Region actions
CodePipeline requires an artifact store in every Region where the pipeline runs actions. So a cross-Region pipeline defines one artifact store per Region (the `artifactStores` map in the pipeline structure, one entry per Region with its bucket and key). CodePipeline copies the artifact into the target Region's bucket before that action runs.
- A standard KMS key lives in a single Region, so the target Region needs its own key.
- That key's policy must allow `kms:Decrypt` (and the S3 permissions must allow `s3:GetObject`) for the roles that read the artifact, such as the CodeDeploy or CloudFormation action role.
Example: pipeline in `us-east-1`, deploy in `eu-west-1` → a bucket and key in `eu-west-1`, with the deploy role in the key policy.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Switch to SSE-S3:** the claim is false (multi-Region KMS keys exist, and per-Region keys work fine), and changing the encryption type does not create the Regional artifact store that a cross-Region action needs.
- ✗ **B. GetObject only:** objects encrypted with SSE-KMS can be read only by a caller that also has `kms:Decrypt` on the key, so dropping KMS permissions causes access denied rather than fixing it.
- ✓ **C. Per-Region artifact store with decrypt grants (correct):** CodePipeline places a copy of the artifact in the store of the action's Region, and the reading role can decrypt it only if that Region's key policy allows it. Missing either piece produces exactly this access denied error.
- ✗ **D. S3 Cross-Region Replication:** CodePipeline does not read artifacts from a replica you manage. It copies artifacts itself into the Regional store defined in the pipeline, and replication would still leave the key permissions unsolved.

## Key idea
Cross-Region actions need a Regional artifact store (bucket plus key) that the action's role can decrypt; changing encryption type or adding replication does not fix it.
Q001216:
## Getting secrets into a CodeBuild build
CodeBuild environment variables have a **type**:
- `PLAINTEXT`: the value is stored in the project or buildspec and visible to anyone who can read them.
- `PARAMETER_STORE`: the value is read from Systems Manager Parameter Store when the build starts.
- `SECRETS_MANAGER`: the value is read from AWS Secrets Manager when the build starts.
In a buildspec this looks like `env: secrets-manager: DB_PASSWORD: prod/db:password`, where `prod/db` is the secret name and `password` is a JSON key inside it.
## Rotation in Secrets Manager
Secrets Manager has built-in rotation for Amazon RDS databases: you turn it on, choose a schedule such as every 30 days, and a rotation function changes the password in the database and in the secret together.
Because the build fetches the secret by name at start time, every build automatically gets the current password and the buildspec never changes.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Parameter Store with a custom Lambda:** Parameter Store has no native rotation, so you must write, test and maintain a function that changes the database password and the parameter consistently. That is more operational overhead.
- ✓ **B. Secrets Manager with RDS rotation (correct):** rotation is a managed feature for RDS credentials, and the `secrets-manager` reference always resolves to the latest value, so the 30-day rotation needs no buildspec edits and no custom code.
- ✗ **C. Plaintext in buildspec.yml:** the password sits in the repository and its history, and every rotation requires a commit, which is exactly the change the requirement forbids.
- ✗ **D. File in a private S3 bucket:** S3 has no rotation, so someone must update the file and the database password together, and the build needs extra download and parsing logic.

## Key idea
Credentials that must rotate automatically → Secrets Manager with managed rotation, referenced by name from the buildspec so every build gets the current value.
Q001217:
## Connecting CodePipeline to GitHub
AWS CodeConnections (formerly AWS CodeStar Connections) links AWS to GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket through an installed **GitHub App**. You authorize the app once in GitHub; AWS stores a connection resource, not a password or token that you manage.
- The pipeline's source action (`CodeStarSourceConnection`) references the connection ARN, repository and branch.
- GitHub sends events to AWS when a push happens, so the pipeline starts within seconds.
- In V2 pipelines, triggers can filter by branch, tag or file path.
## The older options
The **GitHub version 1** action is a legacy action that authenticates with an OAuth or personal access token and is not recommended. **Polling** checks the repository on a timer, which adds delay and API traffic.
Example: a push to `main` in `org/app` fires an event through the connection and starts the pipeline for that commit.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. CodeStar Connections (CodeConnections) source action (correct):** the GitHub App integration triggers on push events with low latency, and there is no long-lived GitHub credential stored in AWS.
- ✗ **B. Polling source action:** polling only notices a change on the next check, so start latency is higher, and it is not the recommended way to detect GitHub changes.
- ✗ **C. EventBridge schedule every 5 minutes:** a timer starts the pipeline whether or not anything changed and can lag up to 5 minutes behind a push; it also does not tell the pipeline which commit to build.
- ✗ **D. GitHub version 1 with a personal access token:** this legacy action depends on exactly the long-lived token the requirement forbids, and storing it as a pipeline parameter exposes it further.

## Key idea
GitHub source with fast triggers and no stored tokens → a CodeConnections source action; polling, schedules and PAT-based v1 actions are slower or less secure.
Q001218:
## Two places to keep configuration and secrets
**Systems Manager Parameter Store** holds key-value parameters. A `SecureString` parameter is encrypted with a KMS key. Standard-tier parameters have no storage charge (KMS usage still applies), which makes them cheap for static configuration. Parameter Store has no built-in rotation.
**AWS Secrets Manager** stores secrets for a monthly fee per secret plus API calls, and adds managed rotation (for example for RDS, Redshift and DocumentDB credentials) on a schedule you choose, such as every 90 days.
## Choosing per value
- Static connection settings (host names, ports, database names) → Parameter Store `SecureString` or `String`.
- Credentials that must rotate → Secrets Manager.
CodeBuild can read both at build start with `parameter-store:` and `secrets-manager:` entries in the buildspec `env` section, so every project reads one central copy.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Advanced tier with custom Lambda rotation:** advanced parameters are billed per parameter per month, and custom rotation code is exactly what Secrets Manager provides built in, so this costs more and adds maintenance.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** SecureString for static values, Secrets Manager for credentials: each value goes to the cheapest service that meets its need, and only the rotating credentials pay for Secrets Manager and get its built-in rotation.
- ✗ **C. Everything in Secrets Manager:** the premise is false because `SecureString` parameters are also encrypted at rest with KMS, and paying a per-secret fee for values that never rotate is unnecessary cost.
- ✗ **D. Encrypted environment variables per project:** values are duplicated in every project, updating them means editing each project, and there is no rotation mechanism at all.

## Key idea
Match the store to the need: Parameter Store for cheap static values, Secrets Manager only for credentials that need built-in rotation.
Q001219:
## The manual approval action
CodePipeline has a built-in **Manual approval** action. When the pipeline reaches it, the stage pauses until someone approves or rejects.
- **Notification**: the action can publish to an SNS topic, which emails or chats the approvers.
- **Review URL and comments**: you can set a URL (such as the staging site) and instructions that appear in the notification and in the console.
- **Who may approve**: approving calls `codepipeline:PutApprovalResult`. Grant that action, scoped to the pipeline's ARN, only to the release-manager group's IAM role or policy.
- **Timeout**: by default an approval that nobody acts on fails after 7 days. The approval action's declaration can set a shorter timeout (`timeoutInMinutes`, which applies only to manual approval actions), such as 3 days; alternatively, a small scheduled automation can reject stale approvals with `PutApprovalResult`.
Example: stage `Approve` sits between `DeployStaging` and `DeployProd`, and SNS sends the staging URL to the release managers.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Lambda sleeping until a DynamoDB flag:** a Lambda invocation runs for at most 15 minutes, so it cannot wait days, and you would rebuild notifications, permissions and expiry yourself.
- ✗ **B. CodeBuild polling a ticket:** it pays for build compute while waiting, needs custom ticket integration, and approval rights would live in the ticket system instead of IAM.
- ✗ **C. Step Functions wait with no timeout:** it adds a state machine and custom action for something built in, and "no timeout" directly contradicts the requirement that approvals expire.
- ✓ **D. Manual approval with SNS and IAM-scoped approvers (correct):** it is the native pause point in CodePipeline, shows the reviewer the staging URL, restricts approval through IAM, and has a built-in expiry that can be set to 3 days.

## Key idea
Human sign-off in CodePipeline → the Manual approval action (SNS, review URL, IAM on PutApprovalResult); custom sleep or polling steps rebuild it worse.
Q001220:
## How VPC-connected builds get network access
When a CodeBuild project is configured with a VPC, subnets and security groups, each running build gets its own **elastic network interface (ENI)** in one of those subnets. Every ENI takes one private IP address.
## Counting addresses in a /28
A `/28` holds 16 addresses. AWS reserves 5 in every subnet (network address, VPC router, DNS, one reserved for future use, broadcast), leaving **11 usable**. Other resources in the subnet use some of those too.
- 5 concurrent builds → probably fine.
- 15 concurrent builds → more ENIs than the subnet has free addresses, so some builds cannot get network access and fail.
The pattern "worked before, fails intermittently only after raising concurrency" points to a per-build resource that runs out.
## Fixing it
Use larger subnets (for example `/24`) and spread the project across several subnets in different Availability Zones.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. ENIs exhausting the /28 subnet (correct):** each concurrent build consumes a private IP, only 11 are usable in a `/28`, and failures appear only when concurrency grows, which matches the symptom.
- ✗ **B. RDS connection limit:** a few extra test builds are unlikely to exhaust an RDS instance's connection limit, and hitting that limit returns an immediate "too many connections" error from MySQL rather than a connection timeout.
- ✗ **C. No VPC support for concurrent builds:** CodeBuild supports VPC connectivity for concurrent builds of the same project; the only limit is the IP space and ENIs available in the chosen subnets.
- ✗ **D. Security group rule missing:** a missing inbound rule would block every build, including single builds that previously worked, not only some builds after concurrency was increased.

## Key idea
VPC-connected builds each consume a subnet IP; if failures scale with concurrency, check subnet size before blaming the database.
Q001221:
## The CodeDeploy in-place lifecycle on EC2
The CodeDeploy agent runs a fixed sequence of events. You attach scripts to some of them in the `hooks` section of `appspec.yml`:
- `ApplicationStop`: stop the running app. This runs the script from the **previous** revision, since the new files are not on disk yet.
- `DownloadBundle`: the agent downloads the revision (not scriptable).
- `BeforeInstall`: pre-copy work such as backing up config or decrypting files.
- `Install`: the agent copies files per the `files` section (not scriptable).
- `AfterInstall`: post-copy work such as setting permissions with `chmod` or `chown`.
- `ApplicationStart`: start the new version.
- `ValidateService`: verify it works; a script exiting non-zero fails the deployment on that instance.
Example: `ValidateService` runs `curl -f http://localhost/health`, which exits non-zero on an HTTP error.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. AfterInstall before BeforeInstall:** permissions cannot be set on files that have not been copied yet, and validating the service before starting it would always fail.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** ApplicationStop, BeforeInstall, AfterInstall, ApplicationStart, ValidateService: this is the real order of the scriptable hooks and maps each task to the hook designed for it: stop, back up, set permissions, start, verify.
- ✗ **C. DownloadBundle and Install as hooks:** these events are reserved for the CodeDeploy agent and cannot run your scripts, and this sequence also leaves out stopping the old app and the health check.
- ✗ **D. BeforeInstall before ApplicationStop:** CodeDeploy always runs ApplicationStop first, and AfterInstall cannot come after ApplicationStart because files must be in place before the app starts.

## Key idea
In-place hook order is Stop → BeforeInstall → (Install) → AfterInstall → Start → ValidateService; DownloadBundle and Install belong to the agent.
Q001222:
## What changes when leaving Jenkins
A self-managed Jenkins setup means patching the controller, managing agents, plugins and disk space. The AWS-native replacement splits that work between managed services:
- **CodePipeline** models the flow: source, build, test, approval and deploy stages, which correspond to the stages in a `Jenkinsfile`.
- **CodeBuild** runs the commands in fresh managed containers, driven by a `buildspec.yml` with phases such as `install`, `pre_build`, `build` and `post_build`.
## Keeping test logic with little rework
Most Jenkins stages already call scripts or tools (`mvn test`, `npm test`, `pytest`). Those commands move into buildspec phases largely unchanged; what is rewritten is only the orchestration around them.
Example: a Jenkins stage `sh 'npm ci && npm test'` becomes `build: commands: - npm ci - npm test` in a CodeBuild project used by the pipeline's Test stage.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. CodeStar converting Jenkinsfiles:** CodeStar never offered Jenkinsfile conversion, and the service has been discontinued, so no automatic "no changes" migration exists.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** Translate Jenkins logic into buildspec commands and CodePipeline stages: the existing test commands are reused inside CodeBuild, while the managed services remove the servers the team had to operate.
- ✗ **C. Jenkins controller inside CodeBuild:** CodeBuild runs short-lived build containers with a maximum timeout, not a long-running server, and the team would still own the Jenkins controller, plugins and configuration.
- ✗ **D. Lambda functions for every stage:** Lambda stops after 15 minutes and has no build environment, artifact handling or pipeline orchestration, so test suites would have to be rewritten and chained by hand.

## Key idea
Moving off Jenkins means reusing the test commands in buildspec files and rebuilding the flow as CodePipeline stages; there is no automatic converter.
Q001223:
## What a permissions boundary does
A **permissions boundary** is a managed policy attached to an IAM user or role that sets the **maximum** permissions it can have. It grants nothing by itself.
For a request to be allowed, the action must be allowed by **both** the role's identity-based policies **and** its boundary (and not denied by any explicit deny, SCP or other policy).
## Example
- Role policy allows `cloudformation:CreateStack` and `s3:*`.
- Boundary allows `s3:*` and `logs:*` only.
- Effective permissions: `s3:*`. `CreateStack` is denied, even though the attached policy still lists it.
## How CodeBuild uses the role
CodeBuild assumes its service role, and every AWS call made by commands in the build uses that role's session, so all of the role's limits, including its boundary, apply.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. buildspec lists IAM actions:** a buildspec has no section for IAM actions; permissions come only from the service role and other IAM policies.
- ✗ **B. Boundaries apply only to users:** permissions boundaries can be set on both IAM users and IAM roles, and applying them to CI/CD roles is a common guardrail.
- ✗ **C. CodeBuild ignores boundaries:** when CodeBuild assumes the service role, IAM evaluates the role's session like any other, boundary included; no service can bypass it.
- ✓ **D. The boundary omits CreateStack (correct):** effective permissions are the intersection of the attached policy and the boundary, so adding a boundary that lacks `cloudformation:CreateStack` removes that permission while the attached policy looks unchanged.

## Key idea
A permissions boundary caps a role; effective access is what the attached policy AND the boundary both allow, so check the boundary when a listed permission is denied.
Q001224:
## Pipelines as code
Instead of creating each pipeline by hand, describe it once in infrastructure as code:
- **AWS CloudFormation**: a template with `AWS::CodePipeline::Pipeline`, `AWS::CodeBuild::Project` and IAM roles, with parameters such as `ServiceName` and `RepositoryName`.
- **AWS CDK**: the same resources written in TypeScript, Python or another language; a construct such as `StandardServicePipeline` can be published as a library that teams import.
## Why this scales
- The template lives in Git, so every change goes through pull requests and code review.
- A new microservice is one stack deployment with new parameter values.
- An improvement to the template (a new security scan stage, for example) rolls out by updating each stack, instead of editing dozens of pipelines by hand.
StackSets, AWS Service Catalog or a CDK library can distribute the template across accounts.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Export and copy JSON:** each copy starts to drift as soon as someone edits it, and there is no central version to review or roll out changes from.
- ✗ **B. Config rules enforcing stage names:** AWS Config evaluates resources after they exist. It can flag differences but does not create pipelines or keep them version-controlled.
- ✓ **C. Versioned CloudFormation/CDK pipeline template per team (correct):** one reviewed, version-controlled definition produces identical pipelines, and updating it updates every instance in a controlled way.
- ✗ **D. Console runbook:** manual console steps are slow and error-prone, and nothing is stored in version control or code-reviewed.

## Key idea
Many identical, reviewed pipelines → one versioned IaC template (CloudFormation or CDK) instantiated per team; copying, runbooks and after-the-fact checks drift.
Q001225:
## Parameter Store tiers
Systems Manager Parameter Store has two tiers per account and Region:
- **Standard**: up to 10,000 parameters, values up to 4 KB, no parameter policies, no storage charge.
- **Advanced**: up to 100,000 parameters, values up to 8 KB, supports **parameter policies**, charged per parameter per month.
## Parameter policies
Policies are attached to advanced parameters only:
- `Expiration`: delete the parameter at a set date and time, such as 30 days from creation.
- `ExpirationNotification`: send an EventBridge event before expiry.
- `NoChangeNotification`: send an event if the value has not changed for a period.
## Throughput
Read rate is a separate account setting: enabling **higher throughput** raises the `GetParameter` limit well above the default, for an extra charge per API call.
Example: 15,000 parameters with 6 KB values and 30-day expiry → advanced tier, plus higher throughput for heavy deploy-time reads.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Split values in standard tier:** splitting doubles the parameter count (pushing further past the 10,000 limit), makes readers reassemble values, and standard parameters still cannot use expiration policies.
- ✓ **B. Advanced tier with expiration policies (correct):** it is the only tier that meets all three needs: more than 10,000 parameters, values over 4 KB, and automatic expiration through parameter policies.
- ✗ **C. Standard tier with a quota increase:** the way beyond the standard tier's parameter count, 4 KB value size and lack of policies is the advanced tier, not a quota request.
- ✗ **D. Move everything to Secrets Manager:** Secrets Manager also has API rate quotas, charges per secret per month, is intended for secrets rather than plain configuration, and does not offer a date-based expiration policy.

## Key idea
Many parameters, values over 4 KB, or expiration policies → advanced tier; heavy read rates → the separate higher-throughput setting.
Q001226:
## Two ways a source action detects changes
**Event-based detection** (the default for CodeCommit sources): an EventBridge rule watches the repository and starts the pipeline as soon as a commit lands on the branch.
**Periodic polling**: CodePipeline itself checks the repository at intervals to see whether the branch has a new commit.
## What polling costs you
- **Start latency**: a push waits for the next check before the pipeline starts.
- **More API calls**: the service keeps asking the repository even when nothing changed, and the calls add up across many pipelines.
- **Less precise**: several quick pushes may be seen as one change.
Polling is still valid as a temporary setting, but AWS recommends event-based change detection.
Example: with events, a push at 10:00:00 starts the pipeline within seconds; with polling it starts only when the next check runs.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. No tradeoff:** polling and events differ in start latency, API usage and precision, which is why AWS recommends event-based detection.
- ✗ **B. Polling is more secure:** removing an EventBridge rule does not improve security; both methods use IAM-controlled access, and the rule only forwards repository events.
- ✗ **C. Polling eliminates cost:** the EventBridge rule for repository events adds no meaningful cost, while polling adds repeated API calls, so polling does not save money.
- ✓ **D. Polling adds latency and more API calls (correct):** the pipeline waits for the next check instead of reacting immediately, and it keeps calling the repository whether or not anything changed.

## Key idea
Event-based triggers start pipelines immediately with fewer calls; polling adds delay and API traffic and is only a temporary fallback.
Q001227:
## Trunk-based development
In **trunk-based development** everyone integrates into one main branch (the trunk) at least daily. Branches, if used, are short-lived: hours or a day or two, and small.
- Small changes merge easily, so there is no "merge hell" from branches that diverged for weeks.
- Unfinished features hide behind **feature flags** instead of long branches.
## Keeping main always releasable
The trunk is protected by automated checks:
- Every pull request triggers a build, for example a CodeBuild project with a GitHub webhook.
- CodeBuild reports the build status back to GitHub on the commit.
- GitHub branch protection rules or rulesets require that status check to pass before merging.
- Each merge to `main` triggers CodePipeline, which delivers the change.
Example: a developer opens a PR with a 50-line change, CodeBuild runs the tests in minutes, the check turns green, and the merge starts a release.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. GitFlow with long-lived branches:** develop and release branches delay integration, so conflicts accumulate and main is only releasable at planned release points.
- ✗ **B. Direct commits with weekly tests:** code reaches main with no verification, and defects are found up to a week later, so main is often not releasable.
- ✓ **C. Trunk-based development with required CodeBuild PR checks (correct):** small, frequent merges avoid merge conflicts, and mandatory build checks ensure only tested code reaches main, so every merge is releasable.
- ✗ **D. Long feature branches merged without CI:** long-lived branches cause merge hell, and merging without CI lets broken code into main.

## Key idea
Every merge releasable + no merge hell → short-lived branches into one trunk, guarded by required automated PR checks.
Q001228:
## CodeBuild webhooks for pull requests
A CodeBuild project with a GitHub source can register a **webhook** in the repository. **Filter groups** decide which events start a build, for example:
- event types `PULL_REQUEST_CREATED`, `PULL_REQUEST_UPDATED` and `PULL_REQUEST_REOPENED`
- `BASE_REF` matching `^refs/heads/main$`, so only PRs targeting `main` build
CodeBuild then builds the PR's head commit and, with build status reporting enabled, posts the result back to GitHub as a commit status.
## Blocking the merge
In GitHub, a branch protection rule or ruleset on `main` lists that CodeBuild status as a **required status check**. A PR whose build failed, or has not finished, cannot be merged.
This runs only the unit-test project per PR, not the whole delivery pipeline.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. CodeBuild webhook for PR events as a required status check (correct):** builds start automatically on PR creation and update, report pass or fail to GitHub, and the required check blocks merging when tests fail, without starting a pipeline execution.
- ✗ **B. CodeDeploy ApplicationStart hook:** that hook starts an application during a deployment; it has no link to pull requests and cannot report a status that blocks a merge.
- ✗ **C. Manual builds after each PR:** people forget, and a manually started build does not by itself block the merge, so failing code can still reach main.
- ✗ **D. Pipeline polling with a full execution per PR:** running the whole pipeline per PR is exactly what the team wants to avoid, and polling adds delay before tests run.

## Key idea
PR validation without full pipeline runs → a CodeBuild webhook on PR events, enforced by a required status check in GitHub.
Q001229:
## SAST as a pipeline gate
**Static application security testing (SAST)** analyses source code without running it, looking for flaws such as SQL injection, hard-coded secrets or unsafe deserialization. Tools such as Semgrep or SonarQube scanners run from the command line.
## How a build fails
In CodeBuild, any command in a buildspec phase that exits with a **non-zero code** fails that phase and the build. A failed build fails its CodePipeline action, so later stages (publishing the artifact, deploying) never run.
Most SAST tools let you set a threshold so the exit code reflects severity, for example a flag that exits with code 1 when any high-severity finding exists.
Example: the `build` phase runs the scanner with its tool-specific fail-on-high option, and the artifact is published only by a later step that runs after a successful build, so a high finding stops the pipeline.
Note that CodeBuild still runs `post_build` after a failed `build` phase, so do not publish from `post_build` unconditionally (check `CODEBUILD_BUILD_SUCCEEDING` or publish in a later stage).
## Shift left
Scanning before publishing is cheaper than finding the same flaw after release.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. SAST in the build phase with a non-zero exit (correct):** the scan runs before publishing, and a high-severity finding fails the build automatically, which blocks the artifact from reaching the repository.
- ✗ **B. Scan in production after deployment:** the vulnerable code is already published and running, which is the opposite of the requirement.
- ✗ **C. Post-build scan reviewed manually later:** the result is looked at only after the pipeline finishes, so the artifact is already published and nothing blocks it automatically.
- ✗ **D. Amazon Macie:** Macie discovers sensitive data such as personal information in S3 buckets; it does not analyse application code for vulnerabilities.

## Key idea
A security gate must fail the build automatically before publishing; a scan that runs later or needs manual review is only a report.
Q001230:
## Performance gates before production
A **performance gate** is a pipeline stage that measures behaviour under load and fails the pipeline when a service level objective is missed.
## Typical design
- Deploy the new version to **staging**, sized like production.
- A load-test stage (a CodeBuild project, or a tool such as the Distributed Load Testing on AWS solution for larger loads) drives the target traffic, for example 10,000 concurrent virtual users with k6, JMeter or Locust.
- Compute the **p99 latency**: the value that 99% of requests are faster than. Publish it as a CloudWatch metric for history.
- Compare with the SLA; if p99 is above, for example, 500 ms, exit non-zero so the action fails and production deployment never starts.
## Why p99
Averages hide slow tails; p99 shows what the slowest 1% of users experience.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. ValidateService during production deployment:** that hook checks each instance after install, typically with a quick health check; it does not generate 10,000 users, and it runs in production, which is too late.
- ✓ **B. Staging load-test stage that fails on SLA breach (correct):** it applies realistic load before production, measures the exact p99 metric the SLA uses, and stops promotion automatically when it is exceeded.
- ✗ **C. Manual local load tests:** a laptop cannot reliably simulate 10,000 users, results vary between runs and people, and nothing stops the pipeline automatically.
- ✗ **D. Monitor production instead:** real users hit the slow release before anyone notices, which is exactly what a pre-production gate should prevent.

## Key idea
Enforce latency SLAs with an automated load-test stage in staging that fails the pipeline on p99 breach, before production sees the change.
Q001231:
## Where custom checks go in CodeDeploy
CodeDeploy runs lifecycle hooks on each instance in order: `ApplicationStop`, `BeforeInstall`, `AfterInstall`, `ApplicationStart`, `ValidateService`. Scripts attached in `appspec.yml` run on the instance through the CodeDeploy agent.
`ValidateService` is the last hook: the new version is installed and started, so this is where you prove it works.
## Example
In `appspec.yml`, the `hooks` section lists `ValidateService` with `location: scripts/check_health.sh` and `timeout: 120`. The script retries `curl -fsS http://localhost/health` for a while and exits 1 if it never succeeds.
## What happens on failure
A script that exits non-zero, or runs past its timeout, fails that instance's deployment. Whether the whole deployment fails depends on the minimum healthy hosts setting, and with automatic rollback enabled CodeDeploy redeploys the last good revision.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Only the built-in ELB check:** lifecycle hooks run any script you provide, so custom health validation is fully supported alongside load balancer checks.
- ✗ **B. ApplicationStop:** this hook runs before the new version is installed and uses the previous revision's script, so it cannot test the new version.
- ✓ **C. ValidateService with a non-zero exit (correct):** it runs after the new version starts, so it can test `/health` on the real new code, and a failing script marks that instance's deployment as failed.
- ✗ **D. BeforeInstall and skipping failures:** the new code is not on the instance yet, and a failed hook fails the instance's deployment rather than being skipped.

## Key idea
Verify the new version in ValidateService, the only hook that runs after the app starts; a non-zero exit fails that instance's deployment.
Q001232:
## Extending CodePipeline beyond built-in actions
CodePipeline has built-in action types for source, build, test, deploy and approval. For anything else you can:
- use a **Lambda invoke action**: the pipeline calls your function with a job ID, or
- define a **custom action type** served by a job worker that polls CodePipeline for jobs.
## The Lambda contract
The function receives `CodePipeline.job` with an `id`. It must end by calling one of:
- `PutJobSuccessResult` → the action succeeds and the pipeline continues.
- `PutJobFailureResult` → the action fails and the stage stops.
If it calls neither, the action eventually times out and fails. For work longer than one invocation, the function can return a `continuationToken` in `PutJobSuccessResult`; CodePipeline then invokes it again to check progress.
Example: the function calls the internal test API, polls for the verdict, and reports pass or fail with the job ID.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. SNS asynchronous trigger:** publishing to SNS starts the tests but never reports back, so the pipeline continues without waiting for pass or fail.
- ✗ **B. Manual approval with a person running tests:** this replaces automation with human work and depends on someone running the tests correctly every time.
- ✗ **C. Only built-in actions:** CodePipeline supports Lambda invoke actions and custom action types precisely for integrations it does not have natively.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** Lambda invoke action with PutJobSuccessResult/PutJobFailureResult: it runs any custom logic, such as calling the test API, and reports a real verdict that gates the pipeline.

## Key idea
Custom gates in CodePipeline → a Lambda invoke (or custom) action that reports the result with PutJobSuccessResult or PutJobFailureResult.
Q001233:
## Build environments in CodeBuild
Every build runs in a container from a **build image**:
- **AWS managed images** contain common runtimes and tools (including some browsers), and AWS updates them over time, so exact tool versions can change and cannot be pinned.
- **Custom images** are Docker images you build and store, usually in Amazon ECR. You install exactly what you need, pinned to specific versions.
## UI tests with Selenium
Selenium drives a real browser through a matching driver, for example Chrome with a ChromeDriver of the same major version. In a container the browser runs **headless**, with no display.
A custom image might install a specific Chrome version and its matching ChromeDriver, plus the test framework. The pipeline's test stage then runs a CodeBuild project on that image that points the suite at the staging URL and publishes results.
Example: `ecr/ui-tests:chrome-126` is used by the project `ui-acceptance`, which runs `pytest tests/ui --base-url https://staging.example.com`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Selenium cannot run in CodeBuild:** CodeBuild runs any Linux container workload, and headless browsers with Selenium are a common use.
- ✗ **B. Default image with cached browsers:** the CodeBuild cache is best-effort and meant for dependencies, not for guaranteeing installed software across unrelated builds, so browser and driver versions would be unpredictable.
- ✗ **C. Local runs and screenshots:** this is manual, not repeatable, and cannot fail the pipeline automatically.
- ✓ **D. Custom CodeBuild image with the browser and driver (correct):** pinned versions make runs repeatable, the tests run headless automatically after the staging deployment, and failures fail the pipeline stage.

## Key idea
Tests that need specific tools and versions → a custom CodeBuild image that pins them, not luck with the default image or cache.
Q001234:
## Why shared test databases break
When several pipeline executions (for different branches) run integration tests against one database at the same time, they read and write the same rows. One run deletes the fixtures another run is using, or two runs insert the same key: failures that appear randomly and depend on timing.
## Ephemeral test environments
The fix is **isolation**: each execution gets its own database, created at the start of the test stage and destroyed at the end.
- A database container started inside the build (for example MySQL in Docker).
- A new RDS instance restored from a seed snapshot, or an Aurora clone, created by CloudFormation for that run.
- A unique schema per run on a shared server, when a full instance is too slow to create.
Every run starts from a known state, runs can go in parallel, and cleanup removes the cost afterwards.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Bigger RDS instance:** more capacity does not separate the data; concurrent runs still overwrite each other's rows.
- ✗ **B. Disable integration tests:** this removes the symptom by removing coverage, so defects in database interactions reach later stages or production.
- ✓ **C. Ephemeral, isolated database per execution (correct):** each run has its own data, so concurrent executions cannot interfere, tests become repeatable, and parallelism is preserved.
- ✗ **D. Serialize all executions organization-wide:** it removes the race but makes every team wait for each other, which slows delivery badly.

## Key idea
Race conditions on shared test data are solved by isolating data per run with ephemeral databases, not by scaling or serializing.
Q001235:
## CodeBuild test and coverage reports
CodeBuild can read test result and code coverage files that your tools already produce and display them in the console as **reports**, grouped into **report groups**.
- Test formats include JUnit XML, NUnit, TestNG, Cucumber JSON and Visual Studio TRX.
- Coverage formats include Cobertura XML, JaCoCo XML, Clover XML and SimpleCov JSON.
## Configuration
Add a `reports` section to the buildspec with one entry per report group:
- `unit-tests` with `files: '**/*.xml'`, `base-directory: build/test-results` and `file-format: JUNITXML`
- `coverage` with `files: coverage.xml` and `file-format: COBERTURAXML`
Each build adds a report; the report group shows pass rates, durations, failing test cases, and line or branch coverage trends across builds.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. X-Ray traces:** X-Ray traces requests through running applications; it does not understand test result or coverage files.
- ✗ **B. CloudWatch Logs Insights queries:** you would parse log text yourself and build the dashboards and trend views, which is the custom work the team wants to avoid.
- ✗ **C. Build badges:** a badge shows only the latest pass or fail status of a build, with no test counts or coverage.
- ✓ **D. Report groups for test and coverage reports (correct):** CodeBuild natively parses the JUnit and Cobertura files and shows per-build results and trends in the console, with no dashboard to build.

## Key idea
Test results and coverage in the CodeBuild console → a buildspec `reports` section feeding report groups.
Q001236:
## Phases versus stages
